title: Chess-match thinking and decision trees
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: How many moves ahead have you prepared?
Jose said that they referred to it yesterday as chess-match thinking, and that before the decision trees he wanted to talk a little about the chapter.

A student said that in the book's example the negotiator was aware of the situation he was in, which helped him later, and that they put his wife on the phone because they knew of a strong connection.
Jose put it into an example: we have a negotiation, you and I, and we have a very big advantage, which is preparation and the tools.
A student said that people only think about their current move, so just taking a little time to prepare knocks out ninety percent of the field. That is his estimate and is to be verified.

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write the next three moves in your negotiation.
Write what the other side might do in reply.
Write the preparation you will do.
Write what you will not rush.

check.q: What did Jose call this way of thinking?
What did a student say preparing does?
choices: Knocks out most of the field

check.q: What did the book's negotiator have?

recap: Think in moves. Prepare more than the other side.
